Jensen Huang, the Taiwan-born co-founder and CEO of Nvidia, had turned a graphics-chip company into the $4+ trillion engine of the global artificial-intelligence boom. His H100s, H200s and Blackwell-class GPUs were the shovels of the new gold rush. Washington treated them as strategic weapons. Beijing wanted them desperately. Export controls—tightened under Biden and later loosened under Trump after Huang’s repeated lobbying—made the chips scarce and valuable beyond measure.
Enter Alice Huang (also known as Huang Le), a Chinese citizen in her early forties. No relation to Jensen. Her résumé, pieced from Chinese databases and corporate filings, showed a swift rise: claimed stints in television (CCTV, Hunan TV—details some outlets could not verify), then HSBC private banking, CITIC Securities, and a Shanghai investment firm. By 2023, as U.S. rules tightened, she sat at the center of Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based data-center/“neocloud” company spun out of the Chinese gaming firm 7Road. Megaspeed became one of Nvidia’s largest Southeast Asian buyers, acquiring roughly $4.8 billion in advanced equipment over two years and renting compute power to customers that included Alibaba. U.S. Commerce Department inspectors had already grown suspicious—equipment still in boxes at a Malaysian site, questions about diversion to China. Singapore and Taiwan authorities also took an interest.
Photos and video placed the two Huangs together. June 2024, Computex in Taipei: Alice seated near Jensen at a bar with industry executives. May 2025: she appears behind him outside a Taipei restaurant after a dinner. Surveillance by U.S. intelligence, according to the New York Times, later revealed communications between Alice and an American citizen who was “unmasked” as Jensen Huang. Officials concluded she had been recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security (MSS) to gather intelligence on the Nvidia chief and potentially influence the company toward more permissive chip sales to China. A secret memo circulated in the Trump administration in spring 2026. Trump himself had been briefed earlier and took no public action. China called the claims groundless smear. Megaspeed and Nvidia long insisted interactions were ordinary customer relations and that no national-security information was compromised.
On 8 November 2026, after the Times reporting exploded, Jensen Huang sent a letter to Nvidia’s employees. “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.” He linked the personal admission to the national-security concerns now public, pledged full cooperation with the board’s independent investigation, and said he loved the country and the company. The board stated it had “no reason to believe” secrets or U.S. national security had been compromised, yet opened a full review. Trump called Huang “a fine person” and said he should stay. The FBI opened its own look. Shares dropped. A shareholder lawsuit followed. Congressional committees demanded a briefing. Alice Huang’s whereabouts became unclear; Megaspeed said it was cooperating with lawyers and inquiries.
The thriller lies in the timing. Huang had spent years in private planes and White House rooms arguing that tighter controls only hurt American companies while China found workarounds. During the same period he was photographed and filmed with the woman U.S. intelligence believed was reporting to Beijing. What, if anything, passed between them—policy instincts, Trump’s mood on the next H200 deal, the quiet architecture of how chips actually move through Singapore and Malaysia—remains unproven in public. Nvidia insists nothing material leaked. Investigators on both sides of the Pacific are still counting the boxes.

videos.title: Inside Theranos with ex-Employee Tyler Shultz
videos.description:
With Theranos and Elizabeth Holmes back in the conversation, we’re revisiting one of the most remarkable firsthand accounts of what actually happened inside the company.

Tyler Shultz joined Theranos fresh out of Stanford as a true believer in its mission. His grandfather, former Secretary of State George Shultz, sat on the company’s board, and Elizabeth Holmes had become a mentor and even a presence at family gatherings. But once Tyler began working directly with Theranos’s technology, he discovered that the reality inside the lab looked very different from what the company was telling the world.

On The Social Radars, Tyler sat down with Jessica Livingston and Carolynn Levy to tell the full story of how he went from employee to whistleblower: the failed blood tests and red flags he uncovered, the culture of fear that kept employees silent, his attempts to raise concerns internally and with regulators, and the extraordinary legal pressure he faced after speaking to The Wall Street Journal.

This episode was originally recorded on December 4, 2024.
